expansion:
A. Crigler massage is right. The lecture calls this “Massage of the lacrimal sac” and explains that it may rupture a membranous obstruction by hydrostatic pressure (L9, slide 22). This fits congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction: the lower end of the duct near the valve of Hasner is the last part to canalize, and complete patency commonly occurs soon after birth (L9, slide 21). The infant’s epiphora and recurrent mucopurulent discharge are also consistent with the lecture’s description of epiphora, eyelash matting, and mucopurulent reflux on gentle lacrimal-sac pressure (L9, slide 21). Initial conservative management is appropriate because spontaneous resolution occurs in approximately 85% within the first year (L9, slide 21).

B. Immediate dacryocystorhinostomy is wrong because it is not the initial treatment described for congenital obstruction. The congenital-treatment slide begins with massage, then lists probing, and describes further procedures only after probing failure (L9, slide 22). DCR is listed separately as treatment for acquired nasolacrimal duct obstruction (L9, slide 29).

C. Topical corticosteroids are wrong because they do not relieve the membranous distal drainage obstruction. The lecture lists topical steroids or other anti-inflammatories for conjunctivochalasis, an acquired cause of epiphora, rather than congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (L9, slide 24).

D. Probing and irrigation are wrong as the best initial choice in this 7-month-old because the lecture presents them after massage in its congenital-NLDO treatment sequence. Probing passes a fine wire through the canalicular system and nasolacrimal duct to disrupt the membrane at the valve of Hasner, followed by irrigation to confirm patency (L9, slide 22). It is therefore an escalation if conservative massage does not succeed, not the first step here.
objective: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction in an infant is initially managed with lacrimal-sac massage because most cases resolve within the first year.
